settings.asyncDelayReason: Asynchronous updates wait this long before they are pushed to the backups. The delay is simulated: it stands in for network latency.
settings.coHostingReason: All nodes run in one backend process. Their messages cross real sockets, but over the loopback interface, not a network.

glossary.label: Detection time
glossary.definition: From the crash of the primary to the first moment any live node's failure detector suspected it.

glossary.label: Failover time
glossary.definition: From that detection to the moment the new primary started acting as primary, after its catch-up and term record.

glossary.label: Time to first update
glossary.definition: From the promotion to the first client update the new primary accepted.

glossary.label: Outage
glossary.definition: From the crash of the primary to the first client update the new primary accepted, measured directly rather than added up.

glossary.label: Recovery time
glossary.definition: From the old primary coming back to the moment it had demoted itself and copied the new primary's store.

glossary.label: Data loss
glossary.definition: Updates the client was told had succeeded that the new primary does not hold at that version or newer, checked when the service is restored.

glossary.label: Expected detection window
glossary.definition: Between the heartbeat timeout minus one interval and the timeout plus one interval after the crash: the last heartbeat may arrive up to one interval before the crash, and silence is checked once per interval. From the failure detector's settings; not a measurement.

glossary.label: Worst-case failover
glossary.definition: Detection plus two promotion attempts, from the configured timeouts. The client keeps retrying at least this long.

notes: Every update, heartbeat, role query and copy crosses a real socket on 127.0.0.1. The nodes share one process, so the network between them is the loopback interface.

In asynchronous mode the primary waits 450 ms before pushing each update to the backups. That delay is simulated: it stands in for network latency, and it is the window in which a crash loses updates the client was told had succeeded.

Synchronous mode confirms an update only after every backup push has finished, and the new primary catches up from the other live backups before taking over, so a crash of the primary loses no confirmed update.
Data loss counts only updates the client was told had succeeded. An update still being retried when the primary crashed is not lost; it is sent again to the new primary.
All intervals come from one monotonic clock in the backend. A crash started on the Cluster page is stamped as the node goes down, slightly late, and is marked so.
For now the new primary is the lowest-numbered live node that is ready; from Phase 9A it will be the leader elected by Experiment 4.
Backups refuse any update stamped with an older epoch than the newest they know, so a returning old primary cannot overwrite newer data even if it misbehaves.
Until Phase 9A this experiment and Experiment 5 share each node's replication service, so a write on the Experiment 5 page can move the primary.
